  ENERGY, CLIMATE CHANGE, ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE, AND RIVER
  COMMITTEE REPORT relative to artificial intelligence (AI) technology and
  services to provide accurate reporting and public disclosure of the City’s
  organization­wide greenhouse gas footprint.

  Recommendation for Council action, as initiated by Motion (Koretz ­ Bonin
  ­ Buscaino ­ Blumenfield):
  REQUEST the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power, and
  INSTRUCT the Chief Legislative Analyst (CLA), with the assistance of the
  Information Technology Agency, Bureau of Sanitation, Port of Los
  Angeles, Los Angeles World Airports and the City Administrative Officer
  (CAO), to report on the feasibility of developing and/or procuring AI
  technology and services to provide accurate and regular reporting and
  public disclosure of the City's organization­wide greenhouse gas footprint,

   A recent report by the Los Angeles Housing Department (LAHD) states that sixty-three percent of Los
Angeles residents are renters, comprising 874,365 households. LAHD further reports that fifty-six percent of
Los Angeles residential households are rent burdened, paying more than thirty percent of their income for rent,
and another twenty-six percent are severely rent burdened, paying more than fifty percent of household income
for rent. In addition to enduring some of the worst affordability challenges in the nation, Los Angeles residential
households faced increased financial hardships during the COVID-19 pandemic.

  Council District 13 has over 101,000 multi-family rental units, the highest number in any Council
District, as well as the highest number of rent stabilized units. According to LAHD, the district also had the
highest number of applications for emergency rental assistance. LAHD paid $321 million on behalf of City
renters under the locally administered Emergency Rental Assistance Programs, with over 57 ,000 approved
applications. High vulnerability areas will require additional support as emergency tenant protections come to an
end, including Historic Filipinotown, Westlake, East Hollywood, Wilshire Center, Little Armenia, and Melrose.

  From the beginning of the pandemic, Council District 13 Rental assistance program was established and
with $1 million from AB 1290 Funds were provided to help 500 CD13 households stay in their homes. To
address the continued need for financial assistance, Council District 13, in partnership with LAHD, will initiate
a rental aid program for district residents. The Council District AB 1290 Fund provides funding for
redevelopment and community services. Sufficient funds are available in the Council District 13 portion of the
AB 1290 Fund for this purpose.

  I THEREFORE MOVE that $3 million in the AB 1290 Fund No. 53P, Account No. 281213 (CD 13
Redevelopment Projects - Services) be transferred/appropriated to the Housing Fund No. 100/43, Account No.
3040 (Contractual Services), for services to support the rental aid program for eligible renters in Council District
13.

Van Nuys Airport is one of the busiest general aviation airports in the United States. It houses
news helicopters, medical transport, and is a critical base of operations for several City
Departments including LAPD, LAFD,, and LADWP. The airport generates over $2 billion in
economic impact for the San Fernando Valley and supports over 10,000 jobs. Yet, with any facility
of this size, there are impacts on the community immediately surrounding the airport. This
includes noise, air pollution, and soot and exhaust being blown into nearby homes.

While much of the airport operations is controlled by the Federal Aviation Commission, the City
of Los Angeles does have some tools at its disposal in terms of land use. The Van Nuys Airport
Plan establishes land use zones for the airport and the land surrounding it. However, this plan
was adopted in 2006 and will soon be out of date. A new specific plan is needed for Van Nuys
Airport to plan for its future and mitigate impacts to the surrounding community.

I THEREFORE MOVE that the Department of City Planning in consultation with Los Angeles
World Airports (LAWA) create a Specific Plan for Van Nuys Airport to replace the Van Nuys Airport
Plan and zoning ordinance 177.327. This plan should:
  • Look at mitigating noise and other impacts from the airport on the surrounding area;
  including a barrier between the airport and nearby homes, additional hangar space, tree
  planting, and setbacks;
  • Establish a community benefit program for the surrounding area;
  • Explore how land covered by the plan can continue to be an economic generator by luring
  new commercial activity.
  • Have extensive engagement with airport stakeholders and local residents;

I FURTHER MOVE for LAWA and the City Attorney to report back on what the city can and cannot
do in terms of regulating activity at Van Nuys Airport.

Since the pandemic, general aviation airports have seen a surge in charter flights as individuals
have been willing to pay a premium to reserve a single seat aboard a chartered flight instead of
flying a commercial airline. This relatively new business model, known as charter by the seat,
has increased significantly at airports across the nation, including Van Nuys Airport. This trend
has been supported by technological advances, such as smart phone applications, that can post
schedules of charter flights and match passengers with available aircraft. As a result,
passengers can access various websites to book individual seats on flights to various
destinations. This practice, while approved under the Part 380 regulations of the U.S.
Department of Transportation, has raised concerns regarding increased operations and
associated impacts to the surrounding community.

Buses are the backbone of Los Angeles' public transit system, comprising two-thirds of the total ridership
on the Metro system. This service is primarily used by very low-income people, with almost 70% of Metro's
riders making around $19,000 a year. Many of these riders live in Los Angeles with 105 out of a total of 119
Metro bus lines (88%) operating within the city. While not directly responsible for bus service, the city of
Los Angeles should do everything it can to ensure that our infrastructure supports the system and offers a
comfortable and fast ride.

Metro has made commitments to improve the bus system, including identifying corridors for quick-build bus
rapid transit (BRT). The agency will also begin work soon on several larger projects within the City of Los
Angeles, including improvements to the Orange Line, the North Valley BRT, and the North Hollywood to
Pasadena Transit Corridor. Metro collaborates with the Department of Transportation on a Bus Speed
Improvement Working Group and has built a number of projects and is planning future projects along
Sepulveda Boulevard, La Brea, and other corridors. Through the STAP program the city will build bus
shelters and other street furniture across the city.

Enhancing the bus system is a very tangible way to improve the lives of low-income Angelenos. Cities
across the world have transformed their transportation networks through relatively low cost improvements
to their bus systems such as the MetrobUs in Mexico City and the TransMileno in Bogota. Through the Rose
Lane program, the City of Portland has created a toolbox of 20 infrastructure improvements to make the
buses of the regional transportation provider faster and more reliable. By making investments to create a
world class bus system, the city can improve air quality, meet our climate goals, and improve mobility for
transit dependent Angelenos.

I THEREFORE MOVE that the Department of Transportation in collaboration with Metro report back with a
plan and strategies to build at least 100 miles of new bus-only lanes within the next five years that focuses
on the highest ridership corridors and most transit dependent communities.

I FURTHER MOVE that Department of Transportation, Bureau of Street Services, Bureau of Engineering,
and Bureau of Street Lighting in collaboration with Metro report back on strategies for improving the areas
around stations and investing in upgrades to the bus network, including:
  • Bus bulbs
  • Full lane markings
  • Mobility Hubs
  • Signal improvements
  •  First last mile improvements

I FURTHER MOVE that Bureau of Street Services and the Department of Transportation create an annual
plan for the next five years of the STAP program, how it can be prioritized along with these bus
improvements and in the most high ridership areas, as well as a budget.

I FURTHER MOVE that DOT in partnership with Metro create a branding and promotion strategy for these
new, enhanced bus facilities.  ...,
